🔴Not every belief that keeps us alive is necessarily true. "Practical usefulness does not imply theoretical truth." ✍ Mostafa Malekian

🔹The fact that a belief helps us in practice, solves a problem, or even contributes to our survival does not by itself show that the belief corresponds to reality. Being useful is one thing; being true is another. You cannot infer the latter from the former.

A medicine may cure our headache, yet the theory on which the medicine was based may not be correct. The drug's effectiveness in curing does not by itself prove the correctness of the theory behind it.

The same distinction must be kept in mind in the discussion of evolution. If we accept Darwin's theory, we must note that the persistence of our beliefs, feelings, emotions, and desires does not necessarily mean they show us the truth; they may have persisted because they helped preserve the survival of our species.

That something ensures the survival of the human species is different from its expressing the truth. We may have held a belief, and that very belief kept our species alive; but from this one cannot conclude that the belief was certainly correct. It is even possible that awareness of a truth, rather than aiding our survival, endangers it.

🔹When people have said since ancient times that "the truth is bitter," one of its meanings is this: what is true is not always life-preserving for us or a guarantor of our continued existence.

🔹Therefore, even if a belief seems perfectly clear and self-evident to us and generation after generation has lived with it, this mere persistence and usefulness does not prove that it is true.

🔹From the fact that "this belief has helped our survival," one cannot conclude that "therefore this belief is true."

🔴Can one be a materialist without denying God? | The difference between materialism and moral materialism ✍ Mostafa Malekian

Materialism comes in two very distinct forms: one is "philosophical materialism" and the other is "moral materialism" or "value materialism." To clarify the difference, we need to see what each one claims.

Who is a materialist in the philosophical sense?

Philosophical materialism is a view of the universe. Those who hold this view believe that nothing exists in the world unless it is the product of the exchange of matter and energy—that is, the product of matter converting into energy or energy converting into matter.

🔹But what about our mind and our mental states? Materialists hold two positions here: Some say that mind and mental states do not exist at all. If we ask why we believe they exist, they answer that this belief is a product of our "folk psychology"; it is within this psychology that something called mind and mental states appears to exist.

🔹Others say that mind and mental states do exist, but they are reducible to the same exchange of matter and energy. In a sense, mind and mental phenomena too seem to be wearing a disguise; otherwise, they too are simply material phenomena.

🔹With such a view, one can no longer believe in the existence of God or a non-material spirit and soul. This is philosophical materialism—a view that many philosophers have held throughout history.

But what is moral materialism?

Moral materialism has nothing to do with philosophical materialism at all; rather, it is a theory in axiology whose gist is this: the only thing that matters in life is wealth.

Here I use "wealth" in a sense that also includes money, property, and assets.

If you believe that in human life only one thing has value, and that is wealth, you are a moral materialist. Since value means having importance, it can be put more simply: in this view, only wealth is important and nothing else in life matters.

According to this view, wealth—for having a good and ideal life—is both a "necessary condition" and a "sufficient condition":

• Necessary condition means that unless you are wealthy, you will not have a good life.

• Sufficient condition means that if you have wealth, you no longer need anything else for a good life.

Most of us human beings, in most historical periods, have not been materialists in the first sense; but the majority of us are materialists in the second sense.

➖From the lecture "Balance and Equilibrium between Money and Spirituality"

"A collection of all good things" is not a strategy

Yesterday I watched the conversation between Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi and Mr. Mohammad Fazeli.

I hold both of these dear gentlemen in respect, and the points Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi made about macroeconomics were certainly instructive for me and all his students (as they always have been).

But at one point in the conversation, Mr. Abdeh Tabrizi said about the 20-year Vision Document: "We drafted this document in 1384, when Ahmadinejad had not yet come to power, and the document's goals seemed achievable."

Linking the failure to realize the Vision Document to Ahmadinejad's coming to power (which certainly dealt a great blow to national interests) does not seem logical to me.

The Vision Document was a completely wrong document from the very beginning. It was a beautifully written essay that had no strategic nature (while an upstream document of this kind should naturally have a strategic nature).

This document was "a collection of all good and attractive things." Strategy is not of this kind. Strategy means letting go of many good things and setting priorities among other good things, and specifying which good thing we are willing to sacrifice for the sake of another good thing.

If these questions are not answered in a document, that document is nothing more than an essay.

I consider it one of my honors that from those very years, when I was teaching strategy, I taught this document as an example of a completely wrong document, and I told my students that this document is not a vision—it is merely eye-catching.

That document was wrong on the first day too; with Ahmadinejad or without Ahmadinejad, for Iran or for Saudi Arabia or for America.

It was a beautiful essay that seemed poetic and attractive. But my judgment is that anyone with even a little literacy in strategy would never have been willing to sign beneath that essay.

The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile. Before that, a battle is already underway — over truth, over assigning blame, over legitimizing military action. Who broke the agreement? Who started the conflict? Who will bear responsibility for the consequences of the next war? The answers to these questions may be constructed and locked in on the media battlefield before the military conflict even begins.

Take the narrative that has taken shape in recent days around attacks on oil tankers and commercial ships: that Iran deliberately violated the Islamabad Understanding and is therefore responsible for the collapse of the agreement and the possible escalation of war. That the attacks occurred is one thing; turning that into a definitive narrative of Iran's unilateral responsibility — without examining the obligations of the parties, the US naval blockade, and the sequence of military actions — is another. Sometimes, to build a misleading narrative, there's no need to fabricate reality at all; it's enough to select part of the truth and omit the rest.

We have seen this before, too, in attempts to discredit real images of the bombing of Tehran. Some media accounts claimed the images of destruction were staged and that the women seen in the photos were actresses who kept reappearing. An independent review of the images from Sabounchi Street in Tehran refuted that claim. Here, the issue wasn't merely the publication of a false news item; it was an attempt to make the audience doubt reality itself, even when confronted with documented images of destruction and war victims.

In the possible next stage of the war, we must be more vigilant than ever against three phenomena: Misinformation — false information spread unknowingly; Disinformation — fake and distorted information deliberately produced to deceive; and Malinformation — real information used to cause harm, for example by revealing the identity or location of individuals at risk. These three can be deployed simultaneously to sow panic, destroy public trust, deny the realities of war, and prepare public opinion to accept a new conflict.

In such conditions, the war propaganda headquarters, if it exists, must monitor the information space moment by moment and respond with speed, accuracy, and verifiable evidence. Of course, countering information warfare doesn't mean constructing counter-narratives or denying unpleasant realities. The main capital in this battle is public trust, and that capital is preserved only through honesty and transparency.

The war of narratives may, before the military war, produce one crucial outcome: whom the public considers the initiator of the war, whom it recognizes as the victim, and whom it holds responsible for the destruction that follows.
